top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu (P002) remains my first choice on the common criteria. The voice is distinctive and recognisable at the level of the sentence and of the whole structure. He shows formal control over very long structures in the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, and an imaginative project that memory, the body and dream have sustained across decades. The strongest passages, as publicly described, anchor the vision in childhood and bodily life, which is the best evidence I have on emotional and moral range. The citation should rest on the prose, with the poetry only as the lyric foundation, because the poetry is the part of the corpus least accessible in translation. This is a weighing of kinds of distinctiveness, not a finding that Adonis falls short. Adonis (P001) is a very close second. His renewal of Arabic poetic language is serious and fully formed. I would support him if the committee judged the poetic case secure. Both cases rest on translations and secondary accounts, and neither has a settled answer on the later decades. Those limits apply to every non-dominant-language candidate and do not justify P000. Carson (P003) is third: her method is a real through-line, but I find the evidence for breadth and for text-borne achievement thinner. I have not independently verified any corpus. This is a committee recommendation, not the Academy's decision.
recusal_note: none apparent from the profile for Cărtărescu, Adonis or Carson. For transparency, my record on Central Europe and Nazism and my long residence in Prague and Vienna are thematically close to Magris and loosely to Cărtărescu's setting. Magris is not on the slate, and this is context, not a basis for recusal.
